analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to transfer or possess a long list of semiautomatic assault weapons.
analysis.headline: The House never voted: the assault-weapons ban sat in a crime subcommittee for seven months, with 13 cosponsors, before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime to transfer or possess a long list of named semiautomatic military-style guns — rifles, pistols, and shotguns like the Colt AR-15, Intratec TEC-9, and Uzi carbine — while letting people keep any they already lawfully owned. It also gave the Treasury Secretary power to add more weapons to the banned list each year using set criteria, and required serial numbers to show whether a weapon was made after the ban. The bill was introduced in September 1993, sent to the House Judiciary Committee's crime subcommittee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People living with gun violence — especially in neighborhoods where guns like the TEC-9, MAC-10, and Uzi carbine were in heavy street use — would gain a federal ban on transferring or possessing roughly 175 named military-style semiautomatic guns, plus a mechanism to add new lookalike models each year. Future buyers, police, and communities would be the direct beneficiaries; current lawful owners keep what they already have. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any person to transfer or possess each of roughly 175 named semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns, including the Colt AR-15, Intratec TEC-9, MAC-10, and Uzi carbine [S2] [S3]

Requires the Treasury Secretary, in consultation with the Attorney General, to review and designate additional semiautomatic firearms as assault weapons every year, so manufacturers could not simply rename or slightly modify banned guns to evade the list [S2] [S3]

Uses concrete criteria — detachable magazines plus features like folding stocks, pistol grips, flash suppressors, and grenade launcher mounts, judged against 'sporting purposes' — so the ban reaches copycat weapons rather than only the models named in 1993 [S3]
Requires serial numbers on covered weapons to clearly show whether they were made or imported after the ban took effect, making illegal post-ban guns easier for police to identify [S2] [S3]
Protects existing lawful owners with a grandfather clause: anyone who lawfully possessed a weapon before the ban keeps it, and government agencies and licensed testers are exempt [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Licensed firearms manufacturers and importers could no longer make, import, or sell the named weapons or any firearm the Secretary later designates, and gun dealers could no longer transfer them. Existing lawful owners were grandfathered, so they did not have to give up guns they already owned. Law enforcement would bear the cost of enforcing a new possession ban. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers and dealers of listed models

drawbacks.text: The named-guns list ran to about 175 models, and the designation criteria (a detachable magazine plus two features like a pistol grip or folding stock, judged 'not suitable for sporting purposes') were broad enough that opponents argued ordinary hunting and target rifles could be swept in as the Secretary made annual additions [S3]

Because the bill criminalized possession and not just sale, ordinary gun owners who unknowingly acquired a covered weapon after the effective date could face federal charges, a heavier enforcement burden than a manufacture-and-sales ban alone [S3]

The grandfather clause meant every banned weapon already in private hands stayed legal to keep and could still be resold legally under the pre-enactment possession exemption, so the guns the bill targeted would remain in circulation for decades [S3]
A one-sentence CRS summary and a text-only record give no cost estimates, so the bill's enforcement cost and real-world effect on violence were never publicly weighed by any committee [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit was straightforward: taking the most commonly trafficked military-style semiautomatic guns off the legal market, with a grandfather clause that spared current owners. The main cost fell on manufacturers and dealers of the listed models, not on the public. The design weakness was breadth: the long named list plus an annual designation power with a 'sporting purposes' test gave a cabinet secretary sweeping authority over ordinary semiautomatic firearms, which is the objection gun-rights supporters would press hardest. On balance the bill was a stronger, broader version of the assault-weapons ban Congress enacted that same session in the big 1994 crime bill — which banned manufacture and new sales but grandfathered possession far more generously. The stronger version died without a vote; the narrower one became law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee's crime subcommittee for seven months, the record closed with a pointer to a separate bill, and Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Introduced September 29, 1993 and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S5]
On October 7, 1993 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, which is where gun-control bills commonly go to stall [S5]
On May 5, 1994 the last recorded action was a note pointing to a separate bill, H.R. 4296; no markup, floor vote, or further movement on H.R. 3184 itself appears in the record [S5]
The 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995 without the House ever voting on the bill [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, importers, and dealers were better off: no ban on the listed guns came from this bill, and its owner-level restrictions never took effect. People counting on a broader assault-weapons ban gained nothing from this particular bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms makers, sellers, and owners of listed guns

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; every named supporter — the sponsor and all 13 cosponsors — was a House Democrat [S4], and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-run Judiciary Committee.

industries.note: The bill barred manufacture, import, and sale of about 175 named models and let the Treasury Secretary add more each year, cutting makers off from the fastest-growing segment of the market. Grandfathering existing owners protected them only partly, since future sales were the industry's revenue.
Dealers could no longer transfer the listed weapons, eliminating inventory value and sales. A new possession ban would also have made customer transactions legally riskier.

Owners of named models were grandfathered, so they kept their guns; but the bill criminalized future possession, and the broad designation criteria could have swept in common semiautomatic rifles and pistols they might buy later.
